source_text: Quod si ita intulisset, non minus docebatur impia esse quam inepta sententia, qua et comparatio ipsa in diverso proposito personarum stolidissima doceretur, cum res non similes ad collationem venirent, natura videlicet et voluntas, ut in parte mali seminum necessitas poneretur, in parte vero boni studii sola libertas, immo iam non libertas, quoniam non suppetebat facultas eligendi boni et cavendi mali, si naturalis reatus fuisset. Dicit ergo Apostolus, sapiens et eruditus Ecclesiae Doctor, per inoboedientiam exstitisse transisseque peccatum multiplicarique iustitiam.
pass_a_gloss: Which if he had so brought in, a sentence would no less be taught to be impious than inept, by which even the comparison itself in a diverse purpose of persons would be taught most stupid, when things not similar would come to a collation, namely nature and will, so that in the part of evil a necessity of seeds would be placed, but in the part of good a liberty of pursuit alone, nay already not liberty, since a faculty of choosing the good and guarding against the evil was not at hand, if there had been a natural reatus. The Apostle therefore, a wise and learned Doctor of the Church, says that through disobedience sin existed and passed and that justice is multiplied.

lemmas.lexica: LS semen; Blaise bodily seed vs transmitted sin
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse

pass_b_english: Had he put it that way, the statement would have been shown as impious as it was foolish. The comparison itself would be utterly stupid, because the persons were presented on different terms and unlike things were compared: nature and will. On the evil side he would place the necessity of seed, but on the good side only freedom of effort—or rather, no freedom any longer, since the power to choose good and avoid evil would not be available if guilt were natural. The apostle, then, the church’s wise and learned teacher, says that sin arose and passed on through disobedience, and that righteousness multiplies (compare Romans 5:19) (Romans 5:19).

choices.why: Bodily seed of generation; Julian denies it carries a will's sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
